activity_context.topic_title: Computing Partial Derivatives Using the Rules of Differentiation

examples.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the constant multiple rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y\operatorname{ln}⁡x) \\  & =y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x)\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we use the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x) & =y\cdot (\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡x+{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)) \\  & =y\cdot ((2x)\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡x+{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{1}{x})) \\  & =y(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x) \\  & =xy(2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1)\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem: For the function $f(x,y)={x}^{3}{y}^{2}+{e}^{xy},$ evaluate $\frac{∂f}{∂x}$ at the point $(-1,1).$
feedback.worked_solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum rule for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}{y}^{2}+{e}^{xy}) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}{y}^{2})+\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{xy})\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the chain rule and constant multiple rules for differentiation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3}{y}^{2})+{e}^{xy}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(xy) \\  & ={y}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{3})+{e}^{xy}\cdot y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x) \\  & ={y}^{2}\cdot 3{x}^{2}+{e}^{xy}\cdot y\cdot 1 \\  & =3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+y{e}^{xy}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(-1,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(-1,1)} & =3(-1)^{2}(1)^{2}+(1){e}^{(-1)(1)} \\  & =3+{e}^{-1}\end{aligned}
$$
